title: Narakasura's Fall and the Sixteen Thousand Brides
story:
The demon was so vast that he seemed to swallow the sky. That was how Uddhava remembered it — Uddhava, Krishna's friend and trusted adviser — and how he told the story afterward, whenever the court of Dwaraka asked him to speak of the war in the north. Narakasura, whom men called Bhauma, son of the earth goddess, had grown until his body filled the heavens, and the world cowered in his shadow.

He had not always been the terror of the sky. He had been a king, a demon king with the earth's own strength behind him, and strength had become ambition, and ambition had reached upward until he seemed to be devouring heaven itself. And to crown his insolence he had done what no demon had dared in an age: he had carried off the princesses of the earth. Sixteen thousand of them — daughters of kings from every kingdom — seized and shut away in his citadel of Pragjyotisha, beyond mountains and water and fire, where no army of their fathers could follow. The kings who had tried to win them back had broken themselves against those walls and gone home defeated, and the princesses had learned, year after year, that no one was coming.

It was Krishna, lord of Dwaraka, who finally went against the demon. Uddhava, who had served Krishna through all of it, never lingered on the battle when he told the story; he passed over it in a sentence or two, because everyone knew its shape. The demon who had tried to swallow the sky was struck down — and with his fall the gates of his city opened, and the long captivity ended.

And now the telling would slow, because what followed was stranger and sweeter than any battle. The sixteen thousand princesses came out of their prisons into the light. They had been prizes — taken and kept, moved and displayed — and no one had asked them what they wanted since the day their kingdoms lost them. But when they saw Krishna, Hari the friend of the distressed, as the old tellings name him, they did what no one had let them do in all those years. They rose, and of their own will they chose him. They asked to be his.

Krishna did not refuse them, and he did not make them wait. In one moment, in their many houses, he took their hands — the giving of the hand, the vow of marriage, made in every home at the same instant, as though he stood before each bride alone. There was no first and no last among sixteen thousand brides, no careful order of precedence; each one was met as if she were the only one in the world.

And in time each of those houses filled with sons — ten sons in every house, the tellings say, children who carried their father's likeness. The princesses who had entered Dwaraka as rescued captives became the mothers of its future, and the city that had been quiet with their sorrow filled with the noise of children and the bustle of sixteen thousand households at once.

When Uddhava reached this part of the story, the court would sit silent for a while — not at the fall of the demon, but at what came after it. The demon had tried to own the sky and the daughters of the earth, and in the end he had lost both. The sky was clear again, and the princesses belonged to no one but themselves — and to the man they had chosen, each of them, in the same moment that he chose all of them.
reflection: The heart of the story is the princesses' choice. Taken as prizes and held as property, they are given back their will at the moment of liberation: they choose Krishna, and he answers with the full dignity of marriage, present to each of them in the same instant. The tellings' detail that he begot ten sons in every house is the storyteller's way of saying that none of the sixteen thousand was ever an afterthought.
next_story_tease: The earrings the demon had torn from the mother of the gods were already on their way back to heaven.
hero_scene: The freed princesses of the earth rising from their captivity in Pragjyotisha and reaching out to choose Krishna, the friend of the distressed, as the demon's city lies broken behind them.
